title: 缺失的一层：如何让智能体学会设计品味｜Hassan El Mghari，Together AI
author: AI Engineer
content:
Brief Description

Hassan El Mghari, who leads developer experience at Together AI, explains how non-designers can make agent-built applications look intentional instead of obviously AI-generated. Drawing on five years of shipping roughly ten apps a year, he identifies recurring patterns of “AI slop,” presents his Hallmark design skill as a way to codify both negative constraints and visual themes, and demonstrates why rapid iteration with smaller models can rival much more expensive models. He closes with a practical workflow built around saved preferences, strong visual references, detailed prompts, incremental features, and repeated refinement.

Table of Contents

  • Design and UX as a Competitive Advantage
  • Recognizing the Patterns of AI Slop
  • Codifying Taste with Hallmark
  • Faster Models Make Iteration Practical
  • Building Your Own Design Memory
  • References, Detailed Prompts, and Smaller Steps
  • Treat Every Generated App as a Starting Point

Design and UX as a Competitive Advantage

My name is Hassan, and I lead the developer experience team at Together AI. I want to talk about how to make AI apps look good—or, put another way, how to stop letting your agents ship ugly user interfaces.

I am especially passionate about this because I love building AI applications. I have built about ten apps a year for the past five years, and some of them have been tried by millions of users. I think the number one reason many of those apps found an audience was their design and user experience. I want to explain how I approach those disciplines even though I am not a designer.

Together AI is an AI-native cloud platform. We help developers run open-source AI models through an inference API, including chat, image, audio, and vision models. We also let teams fine-tune models on their own data and reserve GPU clusters with hardware such as H100s and B200s for training or inference.

The applications I build are usually simple, often just a single page, but I put a lot of attention into design and animation. One was a logo creator used by about 85,000 people. Another, Make Comics, creates a comic book from scratch with the user as the superhero; at the Together AI conference booth, people could take a photo on an iPad and leave with a printed comic book.

I also built a tool that generates subtitles for videos because I upload frequently to YouTube and Twitter. About 8,000 people tried that one. Other projects include a chat app for open-source models, a site that generates five or six variations of a landing page so the user can choose a direction, and an AI cloud agent that accepts a GitHub repository, starts a sandbox, performs requested work, and creates a pull request from scratch.

The larger point is that we now live in a world where many AI applications look like slop. You can often glance at a site for a second or two and know it was AI-generated. Spending an extra ten or twenty percent of the effort specifically on the interface can therefore become a major competitive advantage.

Recognizing the Patterns of AI Slop

Vibe-coded applications often look alike because they share the same visual tells. There is a purple gradient background, italic text in the heading, and a “scroll to explore” prompt. There are all-caps pills with exaggerated letter spacing, gradient logos, random graphics, and too many emojis. Spacing and padding are often inconsistent as well.

If you study enough AI-generated sites, you can make a list of twenty or thirty recurring patterns. People frequently recognize that a website looks AI-generated without being able to explain why. Learning to identify the individual causes matters: perhaps it is the purple gradient, the style of the logo, the typography, or the decorative graphics. Once you can name those patterns, it becomes much easier to prevent them in your own applications and explicitly tell a model what not to do.

The objective does not have to be the best-designed application in the world. Many people on this design track are far more accomplished designers than I am. My goal is simply to build applications that look and feel good, or at least substantially better than an untouched, one-shot AI output.

Codifying Taste with Hallmark

The first way I have tried to solve this problem is a design skill called Hallmark. It codifies common AI-slop patterns and tells the model not to use them: do not default to a purple gradient, do not italicize the title, and avoid the other patterns that make the result feel generic. I call these constraints “AI slop gates.”

The second part of Hallmark is equally important: it gives the model a collection of distinct themes. I created a set of themes and included them as context so that, when Hallmark is asked to create a website, the model has concrete inspiration instead of starting from a generic default. This is a theme that runs through my entire process: when you give AI models very good inspiration, they tend to perform very well.

I launched Hallmark about a month and a half ago, and more than 10,000 people have tried it. I have focused mostly on landing pages. For example, it can produce a one-shot page for an independent podcast or an invoicing application without many of the usual AI-generated tells.

The results are not necessarily perfect landing pages, but they are much better starting points. In before-and-after examples, a page generated with Hallmark is cleaner, has more thoughtful motion, and avoids the gradients and generic decorations of the baseline. From there, you can iterate toward something excellent. A great deal of the magic still comes from going over the result repeatedly rather than expecting one prompt to finish the work.

Faster Models Make Iteration Practical

Application iteration is extremely important, and people often undervalue smaller, faster models for this phase. I may start an application in Codex or Claude Code to establish the base, then use a smaller open-source model such as GLM 5.2 for rapid refinement.

In my view, GLM 5.2 was the first open-source model that became genuinely strong at design. I compared two landing pages, one generated by GLM 5.2 and another by Opus 4.8, and asked the audience to identify which was which. Only a few people chose correctly. In some respects, the pages were almost indistinguishable. The GLM result arrived much faster because the model was smaller, while the other result cost about five times as much and took longer.

In another comparison, the page that arguably looked more stereotypically AI-generated was the one produced by Opus. A cheaper model still has to be sufficiently capable, of course, but GLM 5.2 is very good for this kind of work. Cursor demonstrated a similar idea with Composer 2.5, an open-source model it post-trained. Iterating with it can feel magical because it responds so quickly.

One image-playground example began as a functional one-shot GLM 5.2 application: enter a prompt and receive an image. The first result still contained plenty of AI tells. With only one or two follow-up prompts, however, it gained a stronger logo, better loading states and animations, more deliberate spacing, and a much more polished overall appearance. Iteration, not the initial generation, created the quality.

Building Your Own Design Memory

Start by becoming familiar with the patterns that make an interface feel AI-generated. When you can describe those tells precisely, you can turn taste into instructions. Instead of merely feeling that a logo is wrong, record what keeps going wrong and how you want the model to handle it next time.

Save those preferences in a skill or a Markdown instruction file such as AGENTS.md. As you build, you develop intuition about what you want and what you dislike. If every generated logo is poor and you always have to regenerate it, add instructions about which logo styles to avoid and which approach to use instead. Do the same for layout, type, motion, and other recurring decisions.

Over time I have built a substantial instruction file that helps me generate better applications. Hallmark is effectively a reusable version of the same idea: if you do not yet have your own accumulated preferences, you can start with a skill that captures them and continue refining from there.

References, Detailed Prompts, and Smaller Steps

If you remember only one thing, give your agents references and screenshots. I rarely build anything now without providing a model with substantial visual inspiration. I maintain an inspiration vault: whenever I encounter a website or application that looks exceptional, I save it.

That collection becomes useful when starting a new product. I may decide that an app should combine qualities from Duolingo and two other products, then paste many screenshots into the prompt. The output is consistently much better because the model has concrete visual evidence to work from.

Longer, more specific prompts also tend to perform better. I often record a voice note for one, two, or three minutes and describe the application in detail: what it should look like, how people should use it, who the intended user is, which text box and image-upload interactions it needs, and what inspiration should guide the result. My prompts are now commonly two or three paragraphs rather than a single sentence.

At the same time, break implementation into steps. If an application needs seven features, do not put every detail into one giant generation request. Start with a substantial foundational prompt and several screenshots, then queue follow-up messages that each cover one or two features in depth. Detailed prompting and incremental delivery work together; a long initial vision does not mean the model should implement every feature in a single step.

Treat Every Generated App as a Starting Point

Many people try to one-shot an application and publish whatever the agent produces. That first output is only the base. It is the developer's responsibility to add context and inspiration, go back and forth with the model, and continue refining the product until it looks and feels good.

Keep the application simple, learn to articulate the visual patterns you want to avoid, preserve your evolving preferences, supply strong references, write specific prompts, split work into manageable steps, and use sufficiently capable fast models to make the iteration loop inexpensive. Design taste is not a mysterious final layer that appears automatically; it is context that you deliberately collect, encode, and apply through repeated iteration.
aiSummary: AI 产品的设计品味可以通过反模式约束、视觉参考和快速迭代，转化为智能体能够执行的上下文。
oneSentenceSummary: AI 产品的设计品味可以通过反模式约束、视觉参考和快速迭代，转化为智能体能够执行的上下文。
summary: Hassan El Mghari 提出了一套实用方法，把主观的设计品味转化为编程智能体可以执行的指令。他先拆解 AI 生成界面的常见特征，包括紫色渐变、斜体标题、装饰性胶囊、千篇一律的 Logo、过多表情符号和糟糕的间距。Hallmark skill 一方面设置约束来阻止这些模式，另一方面提供视觉主题库，让模型同时获得负面边界和正向灵感。多组前后对比显示，Hallmark 能生成更干净的起点；GLM 5.2 与 Opus 4.8 的比较则表明，小模型在设计迭代中也能具备竞争力，并显著缩短反馈时间。最终工作流很具体：把设计偏好写入可复用指令，维护灵感库，提供截图，撰写详细提示词，分步骤实现功能，并把每次一键生成的结果都视为继续打磨的基础版本。

mainPoints.point: 可识别的 AI 模式会削弱产品差异化
mainPoints.explanation: 紫色渐变、斜体标题、通用胶囊和 Logo、过多表情符号与糟糕间距，会让氛围编程界面一眼可辨，并降低用户对产品质量的感知。

mainPoints.point: 明确表达偏好，才能让品味重复利用
mainPoints.explanation: Hallmark 把不理想的设计模式编码为约束，再搭配不同视觉主题，将隐性的审美判断变成智能体可以反复应用的上下文。

mainPoints.point: 具体视觉参考胜过模糊的设计要求
mainPoints.explanation: 由截图组成的灵感库能为模型提供明确的构图和风格依据，效果通常优于只要求它生成一个漂亮界面，却不给任何范例。

mainPoints.point: 快速且能力足够的模型能改善迭代循环
mainPoints.explanation: GLM 5.2 的案例表明，小模型的视觉质量可以接近成本更高的模型，同时响应更快，让高频设计打磨变得更可行。

mainPoints.point: 生成的应用只是起点，而不是成品
mainPoints.explanation: 高质量结果依赖详细提示词、逐项实现功能、保存偏好，并持续针对 Logo、间距、加载状态、动画等界面细节给出反馈。

keyQuotes: 如果给 AI 模型非常好的灵感参考，它们往往会表现得非常出色。
如果你只能记住一件事，请给你的智能体参考资料和截图。
更长、更具体的提示词总是更好。
无论智能体生成了什么，那都只是一个基础版本。
